title: Replay the Call
concept: After this one you can replay a call that went wrong and say which line pinned a name tag on each side.
bookTerm: Crossed transaction, Types I and II
bookIdea: A plain Adult line can be crossed in two classic ways. In Type I the answer comes from the Child and treats the speaker as a parent figure, the classical transference reaction. In Type II the answer comes from the Parent and treats the speaker as a child, the counter-transference pattern.
bookSource: Games People Play, ch. 2; Transactional Analysis in Psychotherapy, ch. 9

opener.setting: Sunday, 21:30, apartment 3B, the balcony. The bus stop is loud below, and the phone is on your knee.

lines.text: “Love, you never call. I sit by the phone every Sunday like a fool.”
lines.cue: her voice thin, the ledger open on her lap

lines.text: “After everything I did for you, this is how you treat your Mum?”

opener.ask: Replay this call. Can you find the name tag Mum pinned on you, and the line that put it there?

rounds.label: Spot, round 1
rounds.intro: How this one works: you replay a call that went wrong. Some lines are a person answering you as if you were someone from the past, and that is a name tag. Tap the name tag that fits the line.

items.text: “Son, you're always too busy for your Mum. Just like when you were small and forgot your lunch box.”
items.cue: bright, a little hurt, talking about the lunch box as if it were last week
options: Mum talks to you as the grown-up you are now
Mum talks to you as the boy she packed lunches for
Mum talks to you as Dad, who always had a reason
items.why: She has put a lunch box in the call, so she is answering a boy who has not grown up yet. The sentence is aimed at you, but the name tag is an old one.

traps.0: A grown-up would hear your week and ask about it. Mum is asking about a lunch box, so she is not talking to the person on the balcony.
traps.2: Dad would say “we're fine” and hang up. Nothing in this line is about money, reasons or silence, so it is not his voice.

items.example:
A cousin at a wedding, an aunt who says: “You still can't carry a tray without dropping it, can you, Julia?” You are thirty and the tray is full of pastries.
She is talking to a child who dropped a tray once, and the tray is not the point.

items.text: “After everything I did for you, this is how you treat your Mum?”
items.cue: the ledger voice, every item already counted
options: A plain question about your week
A bill that you are meant to pay back
items.why: The line is a list of what she gave, with the price still attached. It keeps score, and it expects you to be the one who owes. That is the Boss talking through her, and the Kid in you is what it is aimed at.

traps.0: A plain question would ask what happened this week and wait for the answer. This line is totalling instead.
traps.2: A joke would lighten the call, but Mum is not joking, and she would hear it as a brush-off.

items.example:
A school parents' group chat, a mother who writes: “After all the lifts I've given you, you can't even reply to my message?”
The lifts are being counted, and the reply is what she wants paid.

items.text: “Yes, Mum, I'm a terrible son. You're right, I'll call more.”
items.cue: you say it fast, to end the call before it gets worse
options: A Pilot line, true and checkable
A Kid line that folds to keep the peace
A Boss line that tells her off
items.why: You agreed to a verdict before you had looked at it. The Kid folded, and the quick yes is how a name tag gets pinned on you too, because you have taken the lunch box back.

traps.0: A Pilot line would check the claim: “I called on Thursday and on Sunday. Tell me what you need from the week.” That is true and can be answered.
traps.2: A Boss line would say “Stop it, Mum, I'm not nine.” It is sharp and it is not a fact, and it pins the same kind of name tag on her from the other side.

items.example:
A bus stop, a son who says to his father: “Yes, I'm useless with money, I know.” He has not been asked about money at all.
The fast yes ends the talk and leaves him as the boy in the story.

rounds.label: Play, the week in motion
rounds.intro: Now you replay it. Each line is a volley. Some lines pin a name tag on the other person, and some pin one on you. Choose the line that fits the moment.

items.title: Sunday, 21:34, apartment 3B, the balcony
items.setting: Mum has just called you her lunch-box boy. The phone is hot against your ear and the street is loud below.

beats.text: “You never call. I sit by the phone like a fool.”
beats.cue: her voice goes small on the word fool

lines.text: “Mum, I did call on Thursday. Tell me what the week was like for you.”
lines.outcome: Mum pauses. “Thursday? Oh. Well, the knee was bad.” The call turns to her knee, and it is her week now.
lines.why: You answered the grown-up in her with a fact and a question. Nothing was pinned on either side, and she had room to tell you something real.

lines.text: “I'm sorry Mum, I'll call every day, I promise.”
lines.outcome: Mum sighs with relief. “Every day, love. Good.” She is happier, and you are back in the lunch-box story.
lines.why: You took the blame at face value and promised a daily call you cannot keep. The name tag stuck, and the Kid in you is the one who signed for it.

lines.text: “Mum, you always say that. It's not fair.”
lines.outcome: Mum's voice goes flat. “Not fair? I see. So it's my fault now.” The call cools, and neither of you is talking to the other.
lines.why: You protested like a Kid, which keeps the old pairing going: she is hurt, you are in the dock, and neither of you is talking to the other. It does not show her who she is talking to.

beats.text: “After all I did for you, this is how you treat your Mum?”
beats.cue: the ledger voice, a pencil tapping a page

lines.text: “You're right, Mum. I owe you. I'll make it up to you.”
lines.outcome: Mum softens and reads out the bill: the school fees and the winter coat. You are still listening when the call ends with her ledger open.
lines.why: You accepted the bill as a debt, so the call turned into a payment. That is a trap move, and it ends the scene here.

lines.text: “Mum, I'm not a bill. Tell me what you want from me this week.”
lines.outcome: Mum is quiet for a second. “I want you to call. Your Dad never does.” It is the first honest thing she has said all evening.
lines.why: You named the ledger without arguing with the figures, and asked for the real want behind it. The name tag comes off when someone asks for the want instead of the debt.

lines.text: “Mum, you're doing it again. You always make me feel guilty.”
lines.outcome: Mum takes a breath. “I'm the problem, now.” The line is true, but it leaves her nowhere to stand.
lines.why: The true thing is fair, and it still hands her a verdict on herself. She cannot answer a verdict, so the call drops back into the same loop.

beats.text: “Just like when you were small and forgot your lunch box.”
beats.cue: she is laughing a little, the old story is still funny to her

lines.text: “I'm twenty-seven and I've got a job, Mum. Tell me what you want. Forget the lunch box.”
lines.outcome: Mum laughs, then stops. “Twenty-seven. Hm. Yes. You do have a job.” She sounds like she is seeing you for the first time in years.
lines.why: You named two facts you could check, your age and your job, and then asked for the present. You took the name tag off without shaming her for pinning it on.

lines.text: “Mum, the lunch box was twenty years ago.”
lines.outcome: Mum says, “Everything was twenty years ago, son, that's the trouble with you.” She has the lunch box back in her hand.
lines.why: The fact is true, and it comes from your Pilot. She answers it from her Boss, talking down to a boy, so your line is cut and the lunch box is back in her hand. You can see the name tag and you have not taken it off yet.

items.payoff: Mum reads the bill again and calls you her boy until the call ends. The lunch box stays pinned to you for another week.

fallout.them: Mum hangs up without a goodbye. The name tag stays on, and you can hear her ledger closing.
fallout.you: You say yes to everything. The call ends, and you sit on the balcony counting what you owe.

items.title: Sunday, 21:52, apartment 3B, the balcony
items.setting: Mum is quiet, then starts again. This time the name tag she pins is Dad's, and you feel it land on you.

beats.text: “Your Dad says we are fine. So we are fine. Why do you need to call every week?”
beats.cue: flat, practised, a chair creaking somewhere behind her

lines.text: “Dad says we're fine, Mum. Can we be fine and still talk for ten minutes?”
lines.outcome: Mum says, “Ten minutes. All right.” The line gives Dad one mention and then moves on, and she sounds like herself again.
lines.why: You let Dad's words stand without arguing with them and without folding into them, and you asked for something ordinary. Dad gets one mention and no more.

lines.text: “Yes, Mum, you're right. We're fine. I'll stop calling.”
lines.outcome: Mum says, “Good, good.” The call is over almost before it started, and the name tag is now yours.
lines.why: You took Dad's “we're fine” as the rule and folded to it. That is you accepting the name tag on your own side, and it ends the scene here.

lines.text: “Mum, Dad never says anything. I don't know if we're fine.”
lines.outcome: Mum sits up in her chair. “Don't say that about your Dad.” The call now has a second person in it, and he is not on the line.
lines.why: You put Dad in the room as the thing to be defended. That pins a name tag on him, and she has to step in for him, so the call goes off course.

beats.text: “You never listen to me, the way your Dad never listens to me.”
beats.cue: her voice shaking a little, the old hurt coming up

lines.text: “I'm listening, Mum. What did he do that you still feel?”
lines.outcome: Mum is silent, then says, “He went to the club on my birthday, every year.” It is the first real story of the call.
lines.why: You listened to her and asked about the real event, not the name tag. The conversation moved from Dad's ghost to what actually happened.

lines.text: “Mum, I'm sure he didn't mean it. Don't worry about it.”
lines.outcome: Mum says, “You always say that.” She has been waved off, and she waves back.
lines.why: You rushed to make her hurt smaller in your words, so it stayed the same size in hers. The call stays pleasant for a minute, and the hurt stays where it was.

beats.text: “So you think I'm making a fuss. Like always.”
beats.cue: quiet, final, the call about to end

lines.text: “I don't think it's a fuss, Mum. I think it hurt. I'll call on Thursday.”
lines.outcome: Mum says, “Thursday, then.” It is not a fight, and she has a day to look forward to.
lines.why: You named the hurt as real, and you made a checkable promise. Both sides keep their own voice in the call, which is the whole point of the replay.

lines.text: “Fine, Mum. You're right, I'm the problem.”
lines.outcome: Mum says, “Yes, well.” The call ends, and the name tag is on you for the week.
lines.why: You accepted the verdict on yourself. It is harmless, and it leaves the Kid holding the name tag for the rest of the week.

items.payoff: Dad's voice stays in the call for the next week. You count the minutes until Thursday and feel the name tag on your collar.

fallout.you: You hang up without saying goodbye, because the Kid has taken over and is not willing to answer. Mum sits by the phone.

rounds.label: Analyse, explain it
rounds.intro: Read the replay back. Pick the explanation that fits what happened on the call.

items.text: “Look at the lunch box. Mum answered you as a boy, and you answered her as a Kid who owes. Is the pinning on her side, on yours, or on both?”
items.cue: pen down, looking at you, not at the screen
options: Mum pinned the lunch-box name tag on you, and you pinned a debt-collector's name tag on her
Both of you are simply tired, so there is no pinning at all
You are the only one who can change the call, so the pinning is all yours
items.why: Mum's line put you back in the lunch-box story, and your quick yes took the boy's part and left her holding the bill. That is two name tags, one on each side, and an old Boss-and-Kid pair like this runs on until one of you changes voice.

traps.1: Tiredness can make a call harder, but it does not explain the lunch box. The name tags were in the words, not in how late it was.
traps.2: Your side matters, but you cannot pin a tag on her alone. The replay shows her line doing the first pinning, so the blame is not all yours.

items.example:
A family group call with an uncle who says: “You were always the careless one.” Your cousin answers, “Yes, I'm the careless one,” and the call goes quiet for an hour.
The uncle pinned the first tag, and the cousin's quick yes pinned the second.

items.who: Nadia, with a pen in the air
items.text: “Same plain question, two different replies. You ask Sam: ‘Have you seen my cuff links anywhere? The wedding is on Saturday.’ Reply A: ‘Why do you always blame me? You sound exactly like my dad.’ Reply B: ‘Why can't you keep track of your own things? You're not a child any more.’”
items.cue: she writes A and B on the back of the menu, one above the other
items.prompt: Your question came from your Pilot, aimed at his Pilot. Which pairing describes the two replies?
options: A comes from Sam's Kid, treating you as a nagging dad. B comes from his Boss, treating you as a child.
A comes from Sam's Boss, treating you as a child. B comes from his Kid, treating you as a nagging dad.
Both come from Sam's Pilot, so both are matched replies.
items.why: In A, Sam's Kid answers as if you were a harsh parent, so the voice is a Kid's and the name tag is Dad's. In B, his Boss talks down to you as if you were a child. Both cut your plain question, and the cuff links go unanswered until someone moves back to the Pilot.

traps.1: The pairing is the wrong way round. ‘You always blame me’ is a Kid defending himself against a parent figure, and ‘you're not a child any more’ is a Boss correcting a child.
traps.2: A Pilot reply would say where the cuff links are, or that he has not seen them. Neither reply does that, so both are cuts.

items.example:
A kitchen at six, a sister asks her brother: “Where did you put the torch?”
“Why do you always blame me? You're just like Dad.” The answer comes from the Kid and treats her as a parent, so the torch is never found.

debrief.nadia: Mum answered you as the boy with the lunch box, and you answered her as someone who owes, so neither of you was talking to the person on the line. The lines that worked asked for what was wanted instead of arguing with the story. A plain line can be crossed two classic ways: a Kid answering as if you were a harsh parent, which is the name tag Dad wore in Mum's second call, or a Boss talking down to you as if you were a boy, which is the lunch box. Watch which voice you use the next time an old name tag shows up.
debrief.bookTerm: Crossed transaction, Types I and II
debrief.bookNote: The books call this a crossed transaction. In Type I a plain Adult line gets a Child answer aimed at a parent figure, typified by the classical transference reaction. In Type II it gets a Parent answer talking to a child, typified by counter-transference. Mutual Parent and Child exchanges run on until one person changes ego state.

reflection.prompt: Think of one call or message this week where someone answered you as if you were a child, or as if you owed them. Which line of yours pinned the name tag on, and what would a plain question have done instead?
